What was the purpose of using 'innocent children' in Blake's poems?

Contrary to the idea of original sin, Blake emphasises the natural goodness of all people. He therefore undermines the perception that everyone must eradicate 'sin' and devote their lives to the Church, suggesting therefore that we do not need a grand narrative to live by -certainly not one as shallow as the Church.

Blake uses innocent children to highlight the purity and beauty of humankind before it is corrupt by society. In many ways children are myopic to the world around them and are therefore still at a state where they are undamaged by the forces of the industrialized society and closer to both God and nature.
Why does Blake dismiss the idea of institutionalization?

He believes God, Innocence and Goodness is all naturally within us. Therefore institutions that require priests as intermediaries between man and God, or systems which do their bidding in God's name are both obsolete and corrupt.

Blake believes that institutionalization detract from our natural roots as well as our own natures. This can be seen in his poems, for instance in 'The Chimney Sweeper' there is a distinct negative tone to the poem which is set in a domestic environment. This can be shown by the opening line 'I was very young when my mother died'. This is contrasted by poems such as 'The Blossom', which has a natural setting, that at least superficially is more positive.

Blake does not so much dismiss institutions as he does dismiss the methods of institutions. For example, within the Church he does not counter the idea of God, yet reveals in his poems the shallow ideas of the ministers and bishops and priests. Similarly, he reveals the meaningless of these hierarchies. This is portrayed within 'Holy Thursday,' where the children (who are themselves paralleled with natural phenomena) are seen to transcend the structures of the Church, they 'raise up to heaven.' Consequently, Blake reveals the meaningless hierarchy of the Church, paling in comparison with the might of nature.
